Q: Is it possible to compare the .qm/compiled Qt translation files? A:

QM files are not directly diffable, as they use a compact binary representation. To diff them, we need to convert back to a textual format using lconvert (the default XML output format is a good choice here). For example, using Bash:

diff -u <(lconvert before.qm) <(lconvert after.qm)

Q: Maintaining a SOCKS connection over ssh in Python A:

Paramiko doesn't support listening on a local port and running as a SOCKS proxy, as ssh -D does. Also see issue paramiko/paramiko#955: it looks like a candidate pull request was advanced in 2021 but never completed or merged.

The code you show tries to connect to an existing SOCKS proxy, and then tunnel the SSH connection over it. The error you're getting is because there's no proxy already running on 127.0.0.1:1080.

I'd consider launching ssh as a subprocess if you really need this.

Another option is to try to plug an existing SOCKS server library into paramiko as a backend.

Q: how to create binary and .so using libtool A:

You can "trick" automake into creating an ordinary shared object library, or at least you can if you're using the GNU compiler(s), first tricky bit is to use automake's bin_PROGRAMS parameter instead of its static library or or libtool parameters, name the library like this: bin_PROGRAMS = libMyLib.so then you need to ad the -fPIC compiler flag to AM_CPPFLAGS, then, in configure.ac, define a variable SHARED (or whatever you'd like to name it) and set it to "-shared" - then call AC_SUBST on it, like so: AC_SUBST(SHARED) - then add it to the link line in Makefile.am like this: libMyLib_so_LDFLAGS = $(SHARED) - Obviously you change the "MyLib" part to whatever you'd like to name your DSO. The final tricky bit is to change the installation location, because automake will still "think" what it's creating is an ordinary binary (not a library DSO!), so you want to have automake install it - the "make install" part, in a library directory, for example /usr/lib64 --- And you also need to install any publicly required header files that the library depends on, add those to the "include_HEADERS =" parameter. Have fun!

Q: Can compiler ignore ill formed parts of the template body that are never used A:

When you instantiated an object of the class by writing Foo<int> foo1;, only declarations of the member functions were instantiated. The definitions of the member functions, including the ctor Foo<T>::Foo(T), were never instantiated by Foo<int> foo1; because you've not called (odr-used) that function. This means when you don't use the Foo<T>::Foo(T) ctor, the program is ill-formed no diagnostic required.

This can also be seen from [temp.inst] and temp.res:

The implicit instantiation of a class template specialization causes:

  • the implicit instantiation of the declarations, but not of the definitions, of the non-deleted class member functions, member classes, scoped member enumerations, static data members, member templates, and friends; and

Further, [temp.res]:

The program is ill-formed, no diagnostic required, if:

  • 6.1) no valid specialization, ignoring static_assert-declarations that fail ([dcl.pre]), can be generated for a templated entity or a substatement of a constexpr if statement ([stmt.if]) within a templated entity and the innermost enclosing template is not instantiated, or

(emphasis mine)

If OTOH, you try to instantiate an object of this class template by using the parameterized ctor like say by writing Foo<int> foo2(1);, you'll note that all compilers will start rejecting the program. This is because, now by writing Foo<int> foo2(1);, you're actually using the ctor Foo<T>::Foo(T) and its definition will now be instantiated so this time the program will be ill-formed.

Q: Why is CompileFlags from .clangd file not applied to my VS Code build task? A:

clangd and it's CompileFlags section are only here to inform the language server about how to lint your cpp files, it does not affect the compilation performed by clang.

To keep the two (clang/clangd) synchronized, the logical way is to let clangd be driven by clang, using a compile_commands.json file generated from your clang compilation. See clangd documentation about this. This way you only specifiy your compilation flags once, at compile time. You then only enter `CompilationDataBase: <folder-with-compile_commands.json> in your clangd file.

If you want to keep things (relatively) simple and not go the CMake way as suggested in another answer, you can use clang -MJ<compile_command_entry.json> option to generate a list of json entries in compile_commands.json format as an output of the commilation task.

But it's then your job (albeit a relatively easy one) to concatenate these entries in the actual compile_commands.json array.
